content:
The Incident: From 3 Hours to 7 Days Our central Spark ingestion pipeline feeds user-defined feature tables into our Feature Store, powering over 100+ production ML models. It is built to scale to support data science and business users across teams as our feature platform grows.
The job used to take about 3–4 hours. Then it went up to 4 days. Recently, it ran for over 7 days and never finished.
Job duration over 60 days — Not a slow regression, but a sharp performance drop Initial triage checklist:
Did we deploy a code change? No. Same commit, same configs. Did data volume surge? No. Row count and data size didn’t significantly increase. (I previously wrote a library which monitors just exactly this.) Is the cluster unhealthy? No. Other teams’ Spark jobs finished normally. Is the Feature Store throttling? No. Write latency and error rate were flat. Did the job fail with an error? No stack traces, no OOM errors, no non-zero exit codes. It just ran forever. The Spark UI show active execution:
Active Jobs Out of 40 tasks, 39 finished in seconds. 1 task however failed 177 times and kept retrying. Every task failure logged:
ExecutorLostFailure (executor ... exited unrelated to the running tasks) Reason: Executor killed by driver. Executor’s errors The driver logs showed a heartbeat timeout every ~20 minutes:
Removing executor ... with no recent heartbeats: 149645 ms exceeds timeout 120000 ms So the driver kept killing executors in an infinite loop.
The job already had 16 GB per executor. The tempting fix, throwing hardware and memory at it (this will surely help 🤞):
--executor-memory 32g --num-executors 100 No. This doesn’t help—it blows up the cloud bill 💵. As we will see, more executors do nothing when only one task has data. More memory only buys time before an unbounded heap fills up again.
Business Impact The job runs every few hours to update online features. When it stalls, 100+ production models score on stale data, directly hitting pricing predictions.
The goal was to get runtime back under an hour by fixing the real root cause once and for all.
Investigation 1) The Parquet Midpoint Trap The input was a single ~246 MiB Parquet file. Calling df.rdd.getNumPartitions returned 40, so Spark launched 40 tasks. But per-task metrics made no sense:
One task read all 45,876,936 rows. The other 39 tasks read 0 bytes and finished immediately.
Why?
Parquet files store data in row groups, which form the unit of work for Parquet readers.
Spark doesn’t seem know the total number of row groups when it plans. Getting it would mean opening every file and seeking to the end of each one for its footer. For multiple files on object storage like AWS S3, that can take time. I assume that’s the trade Spark made.
Instead, when Spark plans file splits, it calculates byte ranges based on file metadata via FilePartition.maxSplitBytes:
def maxSplitBytes(sparkSession: SparkSession, selectedPartitions: Seq[PartitionDirectory]): Long = { val defaultMaxSplitBytes = sparkSession.sessionState.conf.filesMaxPartitionBytes // 128 MiB val openCostInBytes = sparkSession.sessionState.conf.filesOpenCostInBytes // 4 MiB val minPartitionNum = sparkSession.sessionState.conf.filesMinPartitionNum .getOrElse(sparkSession.leafNodeDefaultParallelism) // 40 val totalBytes = selectedPartitions.flatMap(_.files.map(_.getLen + openCostInBytes)).sum val bytesPerCore = totalBytes / minPartitionNum Math.min(defaultMaxSplitBytes, Math.max(openCostInBytes, bytesPerCore)) } Each byte range is assigned to 1 task.
The actual read parallelism reckoning comes at read time, when Spark passes a task’s byte range to the Parquet reader in SpecificParquetRecordReaderBase.initialize:
ParquetReadOptions options = HadoopReadOptions .builder(configuration, file) .withRange(split.getStart(), split.getStart() + split.getLength()) // <-- the whole story .build(); At read time, parquet-java determines which task owns a row group using a midpoint test in ParquetMetadataConverter.filterFileMetaDataByMidpoint:
long midPoint = startIndex + totalSize / 2; if (filter.contains(midPoint)) { newRowGroups.add(rowGroup); } A task only reads a row group if its byte range covers the row group’s midpoint:
In our case, the parquet file held exactly 1 row group:
This explains why 1 task did all the work, even though 40 tasks were allocated.
2) The Unbounded Future Buffer The skew explains the imbalance, but it doesn’t explain why an executor with a 16 GB can’t grind through 45.8 million rows however slowly.
So I took a few thread dumps from an executor before dying, and all pointed to:
"Executor task launch worker for task 5.260 in stage 809.0" RUNNABLE scala.concurrent.impl.Promise$DefaultPromise.onComplete(Promise.scala:307) scala.concurrent.Future.zipWith(Future.scala:457) scala.concurrent.Future$.$anonfun$sequence$1(Future.scala:671) scala.collection.LinearSeqOptimized.foldLeft(LinearSeqOptimized.scala:126) scala.concurrent.Future$.sequence(Future.scala:671) …
summary: A production Spark job went from 3 hours to 4 days, then ran forever without throwing an error. Here is how Parquet row group midpoints, unbounded Scala Futures, and JVM GC pauses kill the executors.
title: Debugging the 7-Day Spark Job

content:
The Question Thousands of data pipelines. Sooner or later, someone has to answer:
For every job, how much data did this run touch, how long did it take, how much did it cost — and how does that compare to yesterday, last week, last month?
Sounds boring. But it’s also the highest-leverage question a platform team can answer: almost every silent pipeline failure shows up first as a change in one of those numbers.
Mapping SRE Golden Signals to Data Pipelines Google’s SRE framework defines Errors, Traffic, Latency, and Saturation as the foundational metrics for system health.
Signal Data Pipeline Equivalent What It Catches Errors Task failures & retries Crashes, OOMs Traffic Rows & bytes (read / written) Volume anomalies, silent drops, and partial writes Latency Stage & job runtime SLA breaches, data surges, and join skew Saturation CPU, Memory spill, JVM GC Executor starvation and memory pressure 1) Errors “the rate of requests that fail.”
In data pipelines, the common trap is relying solely on orchestrator exit codes. A Spark job can exit 0 while hundreds of tasks fail and retry under the hood.
Example metrics:
failedTasksCount & taskFailureRate: Categorized by reason (ExceptionFailure, FetchFailed, ExecutorLostFailure). 2) Traffic “a measure of how much demand is being placed on your system.”
For pipelines, demand is data throughput—rows and bytes in and out, tagged by source, direction, and user.
Example metrics:
inputBytesRead & inputRecordsRead: Volume per input scan (S3, Kafka, Delta, Iceberg). outputBytesWritten & outputRecordsWritten: Volume delivered to destination sinks. volumeAnomalyRatio: Run-over-run record count vs. a rolling 7-day baseline. 3) Latency “the time it takes to service a request,” tracked in percentiles rather than simple averages.
For pipelines, it’s total runtime against business SLAs. But high-level duration only becomes actionable when decomposed.
Example metrics:
jobDurationMs & stageDurationMs: Wall-clock runtimes per job and stage. taskSkewRatio (maxTaskDuration / p50TaskDuration): Direct indicator of data skew. 4) Saturation “how full your service is, emphasizing the resources that are most constrained.”
For Spark, this measures executor CPU, JVM memory, disk I/O, and network limits.
Pipelines rarely fail cold; they saturate first. An executor running out of memory doesn’t crash immediately—it thrashes in GC, spills shuffle partitions to disk before finally throwing an OOM.
Example metrics:
jvmGCTime & jvmGCRatio (jvmGCTime / executorRunTime): Time spent in garbage collection. >10% signals severe memory pressure. memorySpillBytes & diskSpillBytes: Shuffle data that couldn’t fit in execution memory and spilled to local disk. executorCpuTime vs executorRunTime: Low ratio indicates tasks blocked on I/O wait (S3 throttling, network shuffle, slow databases). How to Monitor Across Teams Take traffic as an example. The two obvious approaches both fail.
Anti-Pattern 1: Cron Queries The naive answer: running scheduled job SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(<byte_size>) FROM <table> against every table we care about.
Doesn’t scale to thousands of tables. Every new table is one more entry to maintain. Costs. Scans entire datasets periodically. That bill isn’t free. Not real-time. By the time the cron queries run, the upstream job finished hours ago. Lack of Attribution. A row count reported doesn’t tell which job produced those rows or what it read to produce them. Anti-Pattern 2: User-Land Application Hooks The other obvious answer: push instrumentation down to the user, requiring application developers to explicitly instrument code (e.g., calling df.count() prior to writes)
Optional instrumentation is forgotten instrumentation. In a platform with hundreds of contributors, “every team should remember to do X” is a hope, not a strategy. df.count() isn’t free. It forces an additional materialization pass over the lineage graph unless cached. Now we’re asking every user to think about caching too, which they’ll get wrong. Governance Friction. Two teams tag their metrics differently and we can’t compare them. Both fail for the same reason: they push observability work onto the platform’s users, instead of making it a property of the platform.
What I Built: The Telemetry Library The library takes a different approach: it hooks directly into Spark’s runtime internals to collect telemetry as jobs execute—throughput, stage runtimes, GC pauses, memory spill, and task execution profiles.
Integration is a single registration at application startup:
implicit val spark: SparkSession = SparkSession.builder() .appName("my-job") .getOrCreate() val observability = new PlatformObservability( metricPrefix = "platform.spark.observability", )(spark) observability.register() What does an application team actually get?
One line of code. Register once at session initialization; zero pipeline refactoring. Zero compute overhead. Extracted from Spark runtime internals—no trigger queries, no re-computations, no extra cloud …
summary: A take on observability for data pipelines: which signals actually matter, why per-team instrumentation never works, how hooking into the Spark internals delivers them, and the real incident the resulting tool helped.
title: Data Pipeline Observability

content:
The Legacy HDFS A high-throughput backend service (1000+ pods serving live traffic) loaded data from on-prem HDFS. The service reads data into memory at startup and refreshes periodically in the background, while upstream Spark jobs and upload services produce and write the data.
Requirements The task was to migrate the storage layer from HDFS to S3-compatible object storage. Constraints:
Zero downtime Continuous availability with zero maintenance windows. Decoupled lifecycles Independent objects produced by separate upstream pipelines. A single synchronized cutover was not possible. Zero blast radius Live pricing decisions depend on these data. We have to minimize impact as much as possible. Migration Architecture Because HDFS reads are off the request path, we used the Strangler pattern with shadow dual-reads without risking service latency. The idea is to implement S3 read behind the existing read interface and used dynamic feature flags to route traffic and perform asynchronous parity diffing per data path.
Dynamic per-path feature flag simplified pseudocode:
enum ReadMode { HDFS_ONLY, // Read only from HDFS (instant rollback) SHADOW_HDFS, // Read both, compare byte hash, serve HDFS SHADOW_S3, // Read both, compare byte hash, serve S3 S3_ONLY // Read only from S3 (post-cutover) } public class StorageReader { // ... dependencies: hdfs, s3, config public byte[] read(String path) { return switch (config.getMode(path)) { case HDFS_ONLY -> hdfs.read(path); case SHADOW_HDFS -> { byte[] data = hdfs.read(path); // serve HDFS byte[] shadow = s3.read(path); compareAndEmitMetrics(data, shadow); yield data; } case SHADOW_S3 -> { byte[] data = s3.read(path); // serve S3 byte[] shadow = hdfs.read(path); compareAndEmitMetrics(data, shadow); yield data; } case S3_ONLY -> s3.read(path); }; } } This guarantees:
Instant rollback: Switch back to HDFS in seconds via dynamic config—no redeployment. Granular rollout: Migrateper data path. Migration Phases 1) Plan the Migration Inventory all data to migrate Retire obsolete data Define the migration unit Scope migration per data path rather than per service 2) Build the New Implementation Consolidate reads behind a single interface Implement the S3-compatible client Add per-path dynamic feature flags Toggle per path at runtime without deployments. Add shadow-read comparison Read from both S3 and HDFS in parallel and emit a metric comparing byte hashes. 3) Upstream Dual-Write Enable dual-writing across producers Update Spark pipelines and upload services to write to S3 object storage alongside HDFS. 4) Pilot Migration We migrated a small, representative sample of data across different sizes and read frequencies to test the workflow and uncover issues before full rollout.
Enable the feature flags The service reads from both HDFS and S3, compares byte hashes, and emits diff metrics while still serving verified data. Monitor parity and the new S3 storage metrics Correctness Byte hash match rate Reliability HTTP 4xx/5xx error rates Connection timeouts and socket drops Client retry counts Performance Latency Throughput The pilot revealed two operational issues:
Large object download timeouts: Downloading large objects caused intermittent drops. We fixed this in Large Object Download. S3 cluster instability during pod boot: The new S3 cluster had transient outages, causing pods to enter CrashLoopBackOff because loading data is required for startup readiness. We fixed this in Failsafe K8s Pod Startup. 5) Migration With the pilot fixes deployed, we migrated all remaining data in batches.
Roll out remaining paths under shadow validation 6) Cutover Disable HDFS writes, switch producers to S3-only writes Turn off HDFS shadow reads Monitor post-cutover metrics Zero read/write traffic on HDFS S3 storage metrics Application metrics 7) Shutdown Delete legacy HDFS code & configurations Large Object Download During the pilot migration, small objects transferred reliably, but large objects intermittently timed out during pod startup.
Rather than building custom chunked range request logic, we switched to AWS SDK’s native CRT-based S3 client via S3AsyncClient.crtBuilder().
Failsafe K8s Pod Startup During pilot migration, for some reason S3 storage was unstable which caused pod startup to enter CrashLoopBackOff. To eliminate this single point of failure, we moved the initial data dependency from startup time to build time: a CI step bakes a data snapshot into the Docker image, allowing pods to startup instantly from local disk before polling S3 for asynchronous updates.
References https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/strangler-fig.html
summary: Migrated data for a live service from on-prem HDFS to S3-compatible object storage with zero downtime.
title: Migrating HDFS to S3 Object Storage with Zero Downtime

content:
ML Pipeline Automation Google’s MLOps maturity model is a useful starting point. It defines three levels — manual experimentation, partial pipeline automation, and full CI/CD/CT for ML.
Level 0 — manual training and deployment Level 2 — full ML CI/CD/CT pipeline These diagrams describe an ideal. Real teams have to decide which parts matter most, and where they’re willing to diverge.
Where Our Team Sits, and Where We Diverged Our pipeline maps closely to Google’s level 2, but we diverged in two places that mattered:
A custom Velocity Tool, not a generic platform. Ours targets a specific shape of work: an optimization problem where most wins come from iterating on features, not from swapping out model architectures. A data scientist — or a business user with a feature idea — can take a candidate from “SQL in a notebook” to “running in production traffic” without writing pipeline glue. In-process inference, not a separate serving cluster. Most reference architectures spin up a dedicated model-serving cluster. For our latency budget, that was the wrong trade-off, so inference runs inside the same backend process that serves the request. The price is tighter coupling between the model runtime and the application; the gain is a meaningful latency improvement. The Velocity Tool The Velocity Tool reframes model development as a declarative problem. The user describes the experiment they want — a feature, its source, its evaluation context — and the platform handles the rest: data prep, training, backtesting, packaging, and registering the result for review.
Each experiment is a DAG of containerized steps, parameterized by a single spec. Roughly:
experiment: feature: name: my_new_signal source_sql: | SELECT entity_id, value FROM raw.events WHERE event_date = '${datadate}' dtype: numeric default: 0.0 base_dataset: weekly_baseline evaluation: business_metrics: [primary_metric, guardrail_metric] backtest_window: 28d promotion_policy: requires_human_approval That’s the entire surface area a user has to learn. Behind it: a Spark feature build, a training step that produces a versioned artifact, an evaluation step enforcing shared business metrics, and lineage captured for audit. Experiments run in parallel, scheduled by the platform.
The Extended Lifecycle: Sandbox and A/B Before Production A good backtest number means very little on its own. Backtests can lie about live behaviour, and a model can be statistically “better” while still violating a business rule no one wrote down. So the pipeline has two stages between training and production:
Sandbox A model that passed evaluation is replayed against production data, with platform-enforced checks on the output. The point is to fail loudly on what backtests miss — broken feature assumptions, silent regressions on a data segment that matters. A/B Experimentation Model from the sandbox is then deployed in production, running with a real traffic behind a controlled experiment. The user gets the same business-metric report as in training, now computed against real customer behaviour. Promotion is a human decision, but its mechanics are fully automated. No “rebuild the artifact for production” step, no rewritten glue code. The artifact that won in A/B is the artifact that runs in production. Removing that gap closes off a long list of “almost the same code, but not quite” bugs.
The Hard Part: Knowing It’s Still Working Detecting that a deployed model has quietly stopped doing its job is the unsolved problem of MLOps. Three regimes, not equally hard:
Labels are direct or cheap. Sample outputs, label them, measure performance. Solvable. Labels are absent or biased. Pick a proxy metric that correlates with what you care about and monitor that — knowing the proxy will eventually drift, and you’ll have to revisit it. The problem is reinforcement-shaped. The model’s own actions change the data it sees, so “compare prediction to ground truth” doesn’t apply. Monitoring becomes distributions, business outcomes, and counterfactuals rather than accuracy. Most of our production models live in the latter two regimes. A model that sets a price in a live marketplace, for example, never gets to observe what the optimal price would have been — only the outcome at the price it actually showed. The label we want is structurally unobservable, and monitoring this class of system well is one of the challenging problems in MLOps.
Retrospective Things from building this that I keep coming back to:
The spec is the product. The declarative thing a user fills in is the product. The orchestrator, storage layout, and training runtime underneath are implementation details and should be replaceable without breaking that contract. Standardize the workflow The platform has strong opinions about the shape of an experiment — the spec format, the metrics, the promotion path — and stays out of the way of what goes inside it. That trade is what makes it safe for non-engineers to ship without the platform feeling …
summary: A platform-team perspective on automating model training, backtesting, A/B experimentation, and deployment — so data scientists and business users can iterate on features without becoming an MLOps bottleneck themselves.
title: Building an MLOps Velocity Tool

content:
When we search for products on an e-commerce, the prices are rarely static. Behind the scenes, hundreds of pricing campaigns run at the same time—special mobile app rates, discounts for specific target, or machine learning models adjusting prices.
Before launching a new pricing campaigns to users, we have to test it first: does this campaign actually bring more values?
This is where pricing experimentation comes in.
Unlike a simple frontend A/B test (like testing a new button color or page layout), experimenting with prices happens deep inside backend services on the live search path. We have to evaluate business rules, assign experiment variants, and calculate prices accordinly.
Requirements Functional Requirements Campaign & Experiment Management An internal UI tool for business teams to create pricing rules, set up A/B tests, and go through an approval process before anything goes live. Targeting (Segmentation) The ability to target specific user groups based on request details (e.g., users browsing on mobile, users searching from a specific country, or logged-in members). Allocation Strategies Support for splitting traffic by different keys (e.g., by user ID, time, etc). Metrics Collecting data on which users saw which prices so we can measure the business impact (conversion rates, revenue, and margins). Non-Functional Requirements Low Latency Pricing services handle high request volumes. Checking experiment variant cannot add extra long latency. High Availability & Safety The experimentation system must stay available so A/B experiment is not disrupted. Campaigns, Allocation, Experiment What each one means:
Campaign: The actual pricing rule or discount logic (for example, “apply a 5% discount”). Segment: The target audience eligible for that rule (for example, “mobile users searching in Thailand”). Experiment: The A/B test setup that splits traffic into groups: Control Group (Variant A): Experiences standard pricing behavior (the baseline). Treatment Group (Variant B): Experiences the new pricing campaign. Because a single experiment might test multiple campaigns, or a campaign might be reused across tests, we keep them in separate tables linked together:
Figure 1: Database schema separating campaign rules, targeting segments, and experiment configurations.
In this setup:
The campaign table stores the pricing logic, schedules, and approval statuses. The segment table holds the targeting rules evaluated against incoming search requests. The experiment table links to an allocation strategy that defines how traffic is split. The campaign_experiment table acts as a bridge, mapping which specific campaigns are activated for each variant. Deterministic Allocation Request lifecycle: enriching context, checking rules, calculating variants, and logging Once a search request matches a targeted segment, how do we decide whether a user gets Variant A or Variant B? This process is called allocation.
We cannot query a remote database on every search request to look up or store an assignment—that would add too much latency and introduce a single point of failure. Instead, the service computes the variant locally on the fly using deterministic hashing:
$$\text{bucket} = \text{hash}(\text{entity_id}) \pmod{100}$$
At a high level:
We take an identifier like user_id. We run it through a fast, uniform hash function and map it into a bucket between 0 and 99. For a 50/50 test, buckets 0–49 get Variant A (Control), and buckets 50–99 get Variant B (Treatment). Because this is a stateless mathematical calculation, the same user consistently gets the same variant every time they search without storing anything in a database.
When running 100+ of experiments simultaneously, there are some real-world challenges. A classic one is experiment correlation. Solving these requires more advanced allocation techniques.
High-Level Architecture System overview Integrating Experiments in the Code When people first think of A/B testing in code, they usually picture a basic if/else check:
request = get_request() ctx = get_context(request) # Simple A/B test check if experiment_client.determine_variant("EXPERIMENT-ID", ctx) == "B": plan_b() # Variant B: Treatment else: plan_a() # Variant A: Control This works well if we only have one or two simple experiments. But in real-world pricing where 100+ of experiments run at the same time across different markets, hardcoding experiment names in code doesn’t work. Every new test would require writing code, testing, and deploying.
Instead, the pricing service uses a rule engine:
request = get_request() ctx = get_context(request) # 1. Match request against active campaigns eligible_campaigns = rule_engine.evaluate(ctx) # 2. Check experiment variants and apply rules dynamically for campaign in eligible_campaigns: variant = experiment_client.determine_variant(campaign.experiment_id, ctx) if variant == "B": pricing_calculator.apply_rule(campaign.treatment_rule) else: …
summary: A look at how we run A/B tests on real-time pricing
title: Pricing Experimentation

Why? We want to identify any performance degradation before merging code changes into the production environment. Imagine there is a pull request changing some critical logic in the code in a way that increases latency of a backend service by a lot, and this is detected after deployed to the production!
The Testing Setup So the basic idea of performance regresssion test is to compare the performance between 2 instances of a backend application; 1 from the baseline (curerntly in production build) and another from the candidate build triggered by a pull request (PR) or a merge request (MR).
We also want to ensure the fairness of the test, so the baseline and the candidate versions will be deployed in isolated environment. For this, Kubernetes CPU Limit can be used.
We can also use tools like k6 to run the performance test.
The .gitlab-ci.yml stages: # ... - docker - manual # ... app_docker: stage: docker script: # Build docker image artifacts: paths: # ... performance_regression_test: stage: manual extends: # ... allow_failure: true needs: - job: app_docker variables: # ... trigger: include: - local: .ci/pipelinees/performance_test/pipeline.yaml strategy: depend resource_group: # ... # .ci/pipelinees/performance_test/pipeline.yaml stages: - test setup # Prepare sample requests, build test runner, deploy baseline & candidate to Kubernetes - perf test # Run the perf test by firing requests to the baseline & candidate - cleanup # Clean up the Kubernetes resource - analyze # Analyze the result, workflow: rules: - if: $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_ID - if: $CI_COMMIT_REF_NAME == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH deploy_baseline: stage: test setup # ... deploy_candidate: stage: test setup # ... perf_test_baseline: stage: perf test # ... perf_test_candidate: stage: perf test # ... cleanup_baseline: stage: cleanup # ... cleanup_candidate: stage: cleanup # ... analyze_result: stage: analyze script: # Analyze the result References https://grafana.com/blog/2021/01/27/k6-vs-jmeter-comparison/
summary: Why? We want to identify any performance degradation before merging code changes into the production environment. Imagine there is a pull request changing some critical logic in the code in a way that increases latency of a backend service by a lot, and this is detected after deployed to the production!
title: Detecting Performance Degradation in CI/CD Pipeline

content:
I’ve long believed that reader-writer locks would outperform mutexes in scenarios with multiple readers and occasional writers. It seemes intuitive: allowing concurrent reads while ensuring exclusive writes should, in theory, optimize performance.
So, is a reader-writer lock better than a mutex? It depends!
I decided to write a small performance test for this. And the initial results were not what I expected at all—they were quite the opposite and very surprising. The mutex outperforms a reader-writer lock!? How can this be?
I haven’t yet pinpointed the exact reasons, but I hope to dive deeper into this later.
Test Design In this experiment, I aim to evaluate the contention performance of an object implementing the following interface. Multiple threads will concurrently call read and update methods, and we will measure the throughput of reads and writes.
class MyObject { public: virtual int read(std::array<int, 2>& coordinates) = 0; virtual int update(int dx, int dy) = 0; virtual ~MyObject() = default; }; Mutex The std::mutex class is a synchronization primitive that can be used to protect shared data from being simultaneously accessed by multiple threads.
The std::lock_guard is a template class that provides a convenient RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) mechanism for managing ownership of a mutex.
In this implementation, we use std::lock_guard to get exclusive access to the lock mutex_ for both read and update operation. This means that only one thread can access or modify x_ and y_ at any given time.
// SynchronizedObject.h -------------------------------------------------------- class SynchronizedObject : public MyObject { public: int read(std::array<int, 2>& coordinates) override; int update(int dx, int dy) override; private: std::mutex mutex_; int x_ = 0; int y_ = 0; }; // SynchronizedObject.cpp ------------------------------------------------------ int SynchronizedObject::read(std::array<int, 2>& coordinates) { std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mutex_); coordinates[0] = x_; coordinates[1] = y_; return 1; } int SynchronizedObject::update(int dx, int dy) { std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mutex_); x_ += dx; y_ += dy; return 1; } Reader-Writer Lock In this implementation, we use std::shared_mutex instead. This is the documentation:
Shared mutexes are especially useful when shared data can be safely read by any number of threads simultaneously, but a thread may only write the same data when no other thread is reading or writing at the same time.
// ReadWriteLockObject.h ------------------------------------------------------- class ReadWriteLockObject : public MyObject { public: int read(std::array<int, 2>& coordinates) override; int update(int xDelta, int yDelta) override; private: std::shared_mutex mutex_; // Shared! int x_ = 0; int y_ = 0; }; // ReadWriteLockObject.cpp ----------------------------------------------------- int ReadWriteLockObject::read(std::array<int, 2>& coordinates) { std::shared_lock lock(mutex_); // Multiple threads/readers can read coordinates[0] = x_; coordinates[1] = y_; return 1; } int ReadWriteLockObject::update(int dx, int dy) { std::lock_guard lock(mutex_); // Only one thread/writer can update x_ += dx; y_ += dy; return 1; } The use of std::shared_lock in the read operation allows multiple threads to enter this code section. So multiple threads trying to read won’t contend each other.
Initial Results What a surprising result. In the above settings, the mutexs outperform reader-writer locks!?
What’s wrong? If this is the case, why the invent of reader-writer lock at all?
The Reason After spending some time figuring out, the exact reason is that: the critial section while holding the lock is too short. As a result, the overhead of the reader-writer lock becomes significant, making it perform worse than a mutex in the initial results.
int ReadWriteLockObject::update(int dx, int dy) { std::lock_guard lock(mutex_); // Only one thread/writer can update // If this critial section takes longer, reader-writer lock is more efficient x_ += dx; y_ += dy; return 1; } If we increase the time spent while holding the lock in update function, the result is as what I expected. Now the reader-writter lock starts to outperform the mutex!
summary: I’ve long believed that reader-writer locks would outperform mutexes in scenarios with multiple readers and occasional writers. It seemes intuitive: allowing concurrent reads while ensuring exclusive writes should, in theory, optimize performance.
title: A Curious Case of Mutex vs Reader-Writer Lock !?

content:
Recently, my job has become a bit monotonous, and I find myself missing the challenges and excitement of working with low-level languages like C++. So I start to grow my interest in algorithmic trading. The blend of real-time data processing, sophisticated algorithms, and performance optimization makes this an interesting topic to study.
In this post, I will dive into one of the algorithmic trading engine, explore its architecture, and try to understand how things work under the hood.
1) Architecture Overview The Engine composes of multiple components. The classes in the diagram below are not completed.
As a user, we write an algorithm in the Algorithm class.
The Engine is responsible for creating the Algorithm and all necessary threads. It then delegates the execution to AlgorithmManager.
The AlgorithmManager is where the main loop resides, which seems to oversee the execution and pass stuff to the Algorithm. It uses Synchronizer to pump or feed data into the Algorithm’s onData() method.
The AlgorithmManager’s Run() method gets an AlgorithmHandler as a parameter which has several handlers:
TransactionHandler This defines how the transactions are processed and set the order fill information. It uses Brokerage to perform the task. It also interacts with the Algorithm’s SecurityPortfolioManager, which seems to have the functionality to simulate the fees, slippage, and other trading condition, through BrokerageModel. RealTimeHandler This triggers functions at regular or predefined intervals. ResultHandler This handles the results of the trading, generating statistics, etc. The Algorithm also has access to several entities:
BrokerageModel SecurityManager SecurityPortfolioManager SecurityTransactionManager The Synchronizer has a DataManager which has a LiveTradingDataFeed which implements IDataFeed interface. This LiveTradingDataFeed is where the live data is coming from, and the Synchronizer provides the mechanisum to stream this data to the Algorithm’s onData() method mentioned earlier.
2) Main Loop The main loop of an algorithmic trading engine is where the magic happens. Below is the code reference, but I will try to break it down later:
public void Run( // ... IAlgorithm algorithm, ISynchronizer synchronizer, ITransactionHandler transactions, IResultHandler results, IRealTimeHandler realtime, CancellationToken token, // ... ) { // ... var backtestMode = (job.Type == PacketType.BacktestNode); var methodInvokers = new Dictionary<Type, MethodInvoker>(); var marginCallFrequency = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5); var nextMarginCallTime = DateTime.MinValue; // ... // ... var hasOnDataTradeBars = AddMethodInvoker<TradeBars>(algorithm, methodInvokers); var hasOnDataQuoteBars = AddMethodInvoker<QuoteBars>(algorithm, methodInvokers); var hasOnDataOptionChains = AddMethodInvoker<OptionChains>(algorithm, methodInvokers); var hasOnDataTicks = AddMethodInvoker<Ticks>(algorithm, methodInvokers); var hasOnDataDividends = AddMethodInvoker<Dividends>(algorithm, methodInvokers); var hasOnDataSplits = AddMethodInvoker<Splits>(algorithm, methodInvokers); var hasOnDataDelistings = AddMethodInvoker<Delistings>(algorithm, methodInvokers); var hasOnDataSymbolChangedEvents = AddMethodInvoker<SymbolChangedEvents>(algorithm, methodInvokers); // Go through the subscription types and create invokers to trigger the event handlers for each custom type... // Loop over the queues: get a data collection, then pass them all into relevent methods in the algorithm. foreach (var timeSlice in Stream(algorithm, synchronizer, results, token)) { // ... time = timeSlice.Time; algorithm.SetDateTime(time); // ... // Update the current slice before firing scheduled events or any other task algorithm.SetCurrentSlice(timeSlice.Slice); if (timeSlice.Slice.SymbolChangedEvents.Count != 0) { if (hasOnDataSymbolChangedEvents) { methodInvokers[typeof(SymbolChangedEvents)](algorithm, timeSlice.Slice.SymbolChangedEvents); } // Cancel all orders for the old symbol foreach (var symbol in timeSlice.Slice.SymbolChangedEvents.Keys) { foreach (var ticket in transactions.GetOpenOrderTickets(x => x.Symbol == symbol)) { ticket.Cancel("Open order cancelled on symbol changed event"); } } } if (timeSlice.SecurityChanges != SecurityChanges.None) { algorithm.ProcessSecurityChanges(timeSlice.SecurityChanges); realtime.OnSecuritiesChanged(timeSlice.SecurityChanges); results.OnSecuritiesChanged(timeSlice.SecurityChanges); } // Update the securities properties: first before calling user code to avoid issues with data foreach (var update in timeSlice.SecuritiesUpdateData) { var security = update.Target; security.Update(update.Data, update.DataType, update.ContainsFillForwardData); // Send market price updates to the TradeBuilder algorithm.TradeBuilder.SetMarketPrice(security.Symbol, security.Price); } // ... // Security prices got updated algorithm.Portfolio.InvalidateTotalPortfolioValue(); Recently, feature stores have become essential in the MLOps stack, providing a centralized platform to serve features across training and serving enironments. In this post, I will explore how to run a self-served feature store, leveraging an open source project Feast.
Why? In our team, we have an application that needs to retrieve features for some ML application. At the time there was no feature store provided by the platform team, so we had to roll our own version. Although Feast’s Python SDK already provides a default implementation to interact with various backed databases for the online store, however, in our production setting, most of our backend applications are written in JVM language. So we need a JVM client library that retrieves features from the feature store. 1) Understanding the Feature Store In its simplest form, a feature store is a key-value store that stores computed features for retrieval. Feast however is more like an ecosystem around a feature store; it consists of a few important components:
Registry An object store of feature definitions and their metadata. SDK The library for interacting within the Feast ecosystem. The client library for ingesting and retrieving features from a feature store. Offline Store The storage that stores the ingested data, which is used for producing training datasets. It supports working with historical time-series feature. This is backed by a different storage and compute engine, for example, Spark, BigQuery, etc. Online Store The storage that sores the lastest feature value, for online, low-latency retrieval. This is usually backed by a low-latency database like Redis, Cassandra, etc. Online Serving Service / Feature Server The service that serves online features from the online store. 2) Customizing the Online Store 2.1) Default gRPC Feature Server The default feature server is implemented using the gRPC server, starting with a Google dependency injection framework Guice, that creates a io.grpc.Server instance.
public class ServingGuiceApplication { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException, IOException { // ... final Injector i = Guice.createInjector( new ServingServiceV2Module(), new RegistryConfigModule(), new InstrumentationConfigModule(), new ServerModule(), new ApplicationPropertiesModule(args)); Server server = i.getInstance(Server.class); server.start(); server.awaitTermination(); } } The main logic of the serving service is implemented in the OnlineServingServiceV2 class that implements the gRPC service:
service ServingService { // ... // Get online features synchronously. rpc GetOnlineFeatures (GetOnlineFeaturesRequest) returns (GetOnlineFeaturesResponse); } If we look at the constructor of this class, we will see that it uses an instance of OnlineRetriever to interact with the backed database:
public class OnlineServingServiceV2 implements ServingServiceV2 { private static final Logger log = org.slf4j.LoggerFactory.getLogger(OnlineServingServiceV2.class); private final Optional<Tracer> tracerOptional; private final OnlineRetriever retriever; private final RegistryRepository registryRepository; private final OnlineTransformationService onlineTransformationService; private final String project; // ... public OnlineServingServiceV2( OnlineRetriever retriever, RegistryRepository registryRepository, OnlineTransformationService onlineTransformationService, String project, Optional<Tracer> tracerOptional) { this.retriever = retriever; this.registryRepository = registryRepository; this.onlineTransformationService = onlineTransformationService; this.project = project; this.tracerOptional = tracerOptional; } // ... } This OnlineServingServiceV2 class is created during the dependency injection and the type of the OnlineRetriever (and therefore the backed database) is selected at runtime. If we are to use a different database such as Cassandra, ScyllaDB, etc, as a backed database for the online store, we will have to implement the code here:
public class ServingServiceV2Module extends AbstractModule { // ... @Provides public ServingServiceV2 registryBasedServingServiceV2( ApplicationProperties applicationProperties, RegistryRepository registryRepository, Tracer tracer) { final ServingServiceV2 servingService; final ApplicationProperties.Store store = applicationProperties.getFeast().getActiveStore(); OnlineRetriever retriever; // TODO: Support more store types, and potentially use a plugin model here. switch (store.getType()) { // ... case REDIS: RedisClientAdapter redisClient = RedisClient.create(store.getRedisConfig()); retriever = new RedisOnlineRetriever( applicationProperties.getFeast().getProject(), redisClient, new EntityKeySerializerV2( applicationProperties.getFeast().getEntityKeySerializationVersion())); break; // ... default: throw new RuntimeException( String.format( "Unable to identify online store type: %s for Registry Backed Serving Service", store.getType())); } // ... servingService = new OnlineServingServiceV2( …

In Kubernetes, setting a container CPU limit like cpu: "250m" or cpu: "2.5" is common practice.
But CPUs are physical hardware execution units—how can it be fractions? What does 250m actually mean? Why do services with low average CPU utilization suffer severe p99 latency spikes?
Requests vs. Limits When deploying a container in Kubernetes, we specify resource requests and limits:
resources: requests: memory: "256Mi" cpu: "250m" limits: memory: "768Mi" cpu: "750m" Resource request (Scheduling & Fair Share) limit (Hard Enforcement) CPU Used by kube-scheduler to place the Pod without exceeding node capacity. Workloads are allocated CPU time proportionally when the node is contested, but can burst if spare cycles exist. A hard ceiling per scheduling interval enforced by CFS Bandwidth Control. If execution time exceeds the quota within the period, the OS kernel forcefully throttles the threads until the next period. Memory Used by kube-scheduler during Pod placement to ensure the node has sufficient memory capacity. A hard ceiling via memory cgroup. Exceeding it triggers the Linux kernel OOM (ExitCode 137). CFS Bandwidth Control Kubernetes limits CPU resources using the Linux kernel cgroup mechanism via CFS Bandwidth Control. The allowed bandwidth is specified by two parameters: quota and period.
cgroup v1: Located in /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu,cpuacct/ as cpu.cfs_quota_us and cpu.cfs_period_us:
cgroup v2: Located in /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max in <quota> <period> format:
Here is how it works:
Within each given period (default: 100,000 µs = 100 ms), the cgroup is allocated up to quota of CPU time. The quota is distributed to per-CPU run queues in slices (default: 5 ms via /proc/sys/kernel/sched_cfs_bandwidth_slice_us) as threads become runnable. If the quota is fully exhausted before the period ends, all threads in that cgroup are throttled and cannot run until the quota replenishes in the next period. When we specify cpu: "250m": $$\text{quota} = 0.25 \times 100{,}000 \text{ }\mu\text{s} = 25{,}000 \text{ }\mu\text{s} = 25\text{ ms}$$
This means your container can consume at most 25 ms of CPU runtime every 100 ms period.
Let’s visualize. Assume a single-threaded task requires 125 ms of pure CPU processing time.
Without CPU limits, the task executes continuously across periods and finishes in ~125 ms: With cpu: "250m" (25 ms quota per 100 ms period):
Period 1: Runs 25 ms $\rightarrow$ Quota exhausted $\rightarrow$ Throttled for 75 ms. Period 2: Runs 25 ms $\rightarrow$ Quota exhausted $\rightarrow$ Throttled for 75 ms. … Period 5: Completes the remaining 25 ms. The task finishes at 425 ms instead of 125 ms—a 3.4x latency degradation:
CFS period vs quota: throttling introduces 300 ms of forced sleep into a 125 ms task Inspecting /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.stat reveals the damage:
Metric Value Description nr_periods 5 Number of intervals that have elapsed. nr_throttled 4 Number of times the group has been throttled. throttled_time 300,000 µs The total time duration for which the group have been throttled. $$\text{Throttled Rate} = \frac{\text{nr_throttled}}{\text{nr_periods}} = \frac{4}{5} = 80%$$
Multi-Core Trap What if CPU limit > 1? This means quota > period. Will it still be throttled?
Real systems run multiple CPU cores. The Linux kernel tracks the quota from the global pool for the cgroup, rather than on a per-CPU basis. So even though the time used in each period per CPU core cannot exceed the period itself, the total sum of quota across multiple cores can be greater than the period. This can result in throttling.
For example, if we set cpu: "2" (quota = 200 ms per 100 ms period) on an 8-core machine, and the application spawns 4 worker threads running simultaneously:
$$\text{Burn Rate} = 4 \text{ threads} \times 50\text{ ms} = 200\text{ ms CPU time}$$
The entire 200 ms quota is depleted in the first 50 ms of the period. For the remaining 50 ms, all 4 threads are throttled simultaneously.
Linux Kernel CFS Code Looking at the Linux kernel scheduler source reveals the exact mechanisms.
1. Slice from the global pool Runqueues (cfs_rq) allocate runtime in a batch fashion (5 ms default slice):
static int __assign_cfs_rq_runtime(struct cfs_bandwidth *cfs_b, struct cfs_rq *cfs_rq, u64 target_runtime) { u64 min_amount, amount = 0; lockdep_assert_held(&cfs_b->lock); min_amount = target_runtime - cfs_rq->runtime_remaining; if (cfs_b->quota == RUNTIME_INF) amount = min_amount; else { start_cfs_bandwidth(cfs_b); if (cfs_b->runtime > 0) { amount = min(cfs_b->runtime, min_amount); cfs_b->runtime -= amount; // <---------- Take from the global pool cfs_b->idle = 0; } } cfs_rq->runtime_remaining += amount; return cfs_rq->runtime_remaining > 0; } To protect the global quota pool across multiple physical cores, the kernel guards runtime assignment with a spinlock:
static int assign_cfs_rq_runtime(struct cfs_rq *cfs_rq) { struct cfs_bandwidth *cfs_b = tg_cfs_bandwidth(cfs_rq->tg); int ret; raw_spin_lock(&cfs_b->lock); /* Acquire global …
summary: Demystifying Kubernetes CPU limits: how CFS quota and period calculate fractional vCPUs, how multi-core throttling happens.
title: How Kubernetes CPU Limits Actually Work

content:
Cache Types 1) In-Memory Cache This uses in-memory data structure to implement a cache, such as ConcurrentHashMap in Java. If we need other functionalities such as eviction policy, then ConcurrentHashMap won’t provide a convenient way to do that. This is where a library like Caffeine comes in.
Advantages
Super fast. Disadvantages
Data is local to the service instance. Limitted by the memory available to the service instance. 2) Distributed Cache Distributed cache typically stores data in memory across multiple nodes or servers in order to scale horizontally. Examples include Redis, Couchbase, Memcached, etc.
This picture is not always correct though! So why not just cache in the memory of the service instance?
Advantages
If cache on service instance, the data will be wiped out every time when the service gets a deployment. Can scale cache independently. Request coalescing. If multiple instances request the same data, distributed cache can deduplicate multiple requests that would have been sent to the backing data store. Disadvantages
Mode complex setup. 3) Client-Side Caching Advantages
Caching on the client side can help reduce server requests Disadvantages
It complicates the analytics as the backend will not receive the request. Will need additional logging in the client to collect metrics. Caching Strategies Read Strategy 1) Read Aside Advantages
Greate for read-heavy loads Only requested data is written to cache Disadvantages
Cache data can be inconsistent if writes are made to database directly. Unavoidable overhead when cache miss (Can mitigate to some extent by cache warming). 2) Read Through Slight different, where the responsibility of the DB read is shifted to the cache.
Write Strategy 1) Write Through Advantages
Data is consistent. Disadvantages
Slower writes; every single write goes to both cahce & database. Some data written to cache is never read; unnecessary cost (Can mitigate by setting TTL to reduce space). 2) Write Back Advantages
Faster writes; writes are only made to cache initially. The writes to the DB is postponed until the modified content is about to be evicted or other cache invalidation policy. Disadvantages
More complex. In case of cache failure, the data may be permanently lost. 3) Write Around In this approach, the application only writes to the DB.
Monitoring We Cache a Cache, that Caches Another Cache! References https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cache_%28computing%29 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/database-caching-strategies-using-redis/caching-patterns.html https://stackoverflow.com/questions/23355136/cache-reads-and-writes
summary: Cache Types 1) In-Memory Cache This uses in-memory data structure to implement a cache, such as ConcurrentHashMap in Java. If we need other functionalities such as eviction policy, then ConcurrentHashMap won’t provide a convenient way to do that.
title: Cache At its Finest

In this post I will be exploring the TFX and its integration with Kubeflow Pipelines on Google AI Platform.
This post is kind of my summarization for my learning purpose.
1) Dataset 2) Create Clusters 3) Understanding TFX Pipelines In order to understand TFX pipelines, we need to understand some keywords. For full tutorial, refer to TensorFlow’s article here.
Artifact Artifacts are the output of the steps in a TFX pipeline. They can be used by subsequent steps in the pipeline.
Artifacts must be stongly typed with an artifact type registered in the ML Metadata store. This point is not very clear yet; I need to research and will come back to expand more on this later.
Questions
Where does artifact get stored? What needs to be changed if we run the pipeline on a Cloud? Parameter Parameters are something that we can set through configuration, instead of hard coding; they are just like the hyperparameters of a ML/DL model.
Component Component is an implementation of the task in our pipeline. Components in TFX are composed of
Component specification: This defines the component’s input and output artifacts, and component’s parameters. Executor: This implements the real work of a step in the pipeline. Component interface: This packages the component specification and executor for use in a pipeline. (This is not very clear.) Questions
Where does the component get run? Do components run in the same environment? Same OS and same dependencies? What if each component requires different dependencies? Pipeline TensorFlow says that a TFX pipeline is a portable implementation of an ML workflow, as it can be run on different ochestrators, such as: Apache Airflow, Apache Beam, and Kubeflow Pipelines.
First, we build a pipeline, which is of type tfx.orchestration.pipeline.Pipeline:
from tfx.orchestration import pipeline def _create_pipeline() -> pipeline.Pipeline: """ """ pass To select a different ochestration tool, we need to import from tfx.orchestration module.
# Airflow from tfx.orchestration.airflow.airflow_dag_runner import AirflowDagRunner from tfx.orchestration.airflow.airflow_dag_runner import AirflowPipelineConfig DAG = AirflowDagRunner(AirflowPipelineConfig()).run( _create_pipeline() ) # Kubeflow from tfx.orchestration.kubeflow import kubeflow_dag_runner kubeflow_dag_runner.KubeflowDagRunner().run( create_pipeline() ) 4) TFX Custom Components Understanding the custom components will get us far! Refer to TensorFlow’s article here.
TFX components at runtime When a pipeline runs a TFX component, the component is executed in three phases:
First, the Driver uses the component specification to retrieve the required artifacts from the metadata store and pass them into the component. Next, the Executor performs the component’s work. Then the Publisher uses the component specification and the results from the executor to store the component’s outputs in the metadata store. Types of custom components Python function-based components
The specification is completely defined in the Python code. The function’s arguments with type annotations describe input artifact, output artifact, and parameters. The function’s body defines the component’s executor. The component interface is dedined by adding @component decorator. @component def MyComponent( model: InputArtifact[Model], output: OutputArtifact[Model], threshold: Parameter[int] = 10 ) -> OutputDict(accuracy=float): """ """ pass Container-based components
This is suitable for building a component with custom runtime environment and dependencies. Fully custom components
This is for building a component that is not in the built-in TFX standard components. It lets us build a component by implementing a custom component specification, executor, and component interface classes. 5) Code 6) Pipeline Dashboard 7) Dataflow My Thoughts TFX seems to be built around TensorFlow. Not very sure if it’s gonna work with other DL/ML libraries without heavily modifying the TFX components. But if we are in a Google Cloud/TensorFlow ecosystem, stick with it! Unlike TFX, MLFlow seems to be more general and more open to other DL/ML libraries. References https://www.tensorflow.org/tfx/tutorials https://www.tensorflow.org/tfx/guide/mlmd

The most successful ML projects in production (Tesla, iPhone, Amazon drones, Zipline) are where you own the entire stack. They iterate not just ML algorithms but also: 1) how to collect/label data, 2) infrastructure, 3) hardware ML models run on.
Summarizing Andrej Karpathy’s CVPR talk, Chip Huyen highlighted that the most successful ML projects in production are those that have complete ownership of the entire stack. These projects iterate not only on ML algorithms but also on data collection and labeling, infrastructure, and the hardware on which ML models operate.
Waymo, another major player, released its dataset in 2019, which is in TFRecord format, requiring TensorFlow for reading. This heavy dependence on TensorFlow makes the tools and data preprocessing pipeline less compatible with other frameworks. In contrast, datasets like KITTI, Lyft, TRI, and Argoverse are released in a simpler, raw format. As someone who used PyTorch more than TensorFlow, I found it difficult to inspect and debug the tf.data components when eager execution was not available inside tf.data.
After a year and listening to Andrej Karpathy’s talk at CVPR 2021, I now kind of appreciate why Google’s Waymo chose to release their dataset in TFRecord format. Interestingly, the winner of the Challenge used PyTorch though.
The good news is… we can now use:
# TensorFlow 2.5 tf.data.experimental.enable_debug_mode() Enough for the introduction, let’s visualize the data.
Visualizing Camera Data Most of the code is straightforward.
import tensorflow as tf import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import matplotlib.patches as patches # Replace FILENAME with tfrecord file dataset = tf.data.TFRecordDataset(FILENAME, compression_type='') for data in dataset: frame = open_dataset.Frame() frame.ParseFromString(bytearray(data.numpy())) plt.figure() # Draw the camera labels. count = 0 for camera_image in frame.images: for camera_labels in frame.camera_labels: # Ignore camera labels that do not correspond to this camera. if camera_labels.name != camera_image.name: continue count += 1 ax = plt.subplot(2, 3, count) # Iterate over the individual labels. for label in camera_labels.labels: # Draw the object bounding box. ax.add_patch(patches.Rectangle( xy=(label.box.center_x - 0.5 * label.box.length, label.box.center_y - 0.5 * label.box.width), width=label.box.length, height=label.box.width, linewidth=1, edgecolor='red', facecolor='none')) # Show the camera image. plt.imshow(tf.image.decode_jpeg(camera_image.image)) plt.title(camera_image.name)) plt.grid(False) plt.axis('off') plt.show() plt.close() The following shows some of the dataset.

content:
“We stand on the brink of a technological revolution. Soon, few of us will own our own automobiles and instead will get around in driverless electric vehicles that we summon with the touch of an app. We will be liberated from driving, prevent over 90% of car crashes, provide freedom of mobility to the elderly and disabled, and decrease our dependence on fossil fuels.” — The Quest to Build the Driverless Car
The same applies to oil and gas industry. Although robotic technologies have entered the oil and gas industry for around some time, the quest to build the autonomous underwater vehicle must go on!
In this post, I will briefly write about the kind of the things we do at our R&D team. (Please note that I cannot write all the details and so I have skipped some parts.)
A System What do we need in order to build an autonomous underwater vehicle and its system?
Hardware Software Navigation software Perception algorithms Planning algorithms Control algorithms Simulation platform Data analytics software All the teams (software, electrical, and mechanical) collaboratively design the robot. The physical aspect of the robot is mainly designed by a mechanical engineer team where they need to consider things such as the dynamic model, hydrodynamic model, robot mechanisms, and etc. The electrical engineer team is the ones who design and lay out electrical circuits connecting all components to a system. The software team mostly look at the high level aspect of the robot such as what sensors, what algorithms, how to communicate with the vessel, how many computing units, how to store logging data, and the list goes on.
Hardware Navigation Software IMU dead reckoning SLAM Map building Perception Algorithms Perception algorithms are probably the key to intelligent autonomous vehicles. At ARV, we have developed several algorithms, including but not limited to 2D object detection, 3D object detection, point cloud-related algorithms, etc., in order to tackle the challenges we encountered in subsea robotics.
We have also developed several machine learning and deep learning models for automatic pipeline inspection as well. These are used both in online (real-time) and offline (data analytics software).
Planning Algorithms Way point planning Optimal path planning Control Algorithms Simulation Platform This is probably the testbed of our robotics software development. We use Gazebo as a simulator for realistic simulation, with some custom-implemented sensor plugins that we developed for our own use.
Of course, these custom plugins should run very fast for the simulation to run smoothly, so the algorihtms must be hevily optimized. For example, the custom sonar plugin was implemented in CUDA to speed things up.
Data Analytics Software The collected data when the robot operates at the seabed must be analyzed in some way. We build our web application where customers can log in to see the analyzed data (as well as raw data) and the generated report.

content:
Introduction This is the first-ever post of my blog; so I will give it a try. This post is about things that I went through when I tried to implement a simple monocular visual odometry from scratch. For a programming language, I choose MATLAB because it is easy-to-use and fast for prototyping a project.
Disclaimer: This is not a state-of-the-art implementation. This simply serves the purpose of learning.
The Problem To give a general idea, visual odometry (VO) is an algorithm that aims to recover the path incrementally, by using the visual input from cameras, and hence the name. It can be considered as a sequential structure from motion, as opposed to hierarchical structure from motion. Imagine a robot or an agent, attached with a calibrated camera $C$, moves through an environment and receives the image continuously. The images $I_k, I_{k-1}$ are taken at different time steps $k$ and $k-1$, which corresponds to the camera pose $C_k$ and $C_{k-1}$ respectively. The task of VO is basically to retrieve the transformation matrix $$T = \left[R \lvert t \right]$$ that relates two camera poses, and concatenate all the transformaitons $T_k$ to get the current camera pose:
$$ C_{t} = T_{t,t-1}C_{t-1}$$ Getting Things Up & Running I first have an initialization function vo_initialize.m that takes two image frames, establishing keypoint correspondences between these two frames using KLT feature tracker, estimating relative camera pose, and finally triangulating an initial 3D point cloud landmarks. I admit that these may sound lacking of excitement (as they are something that is well understood in the computer vision community), but they are not easy to implement from scratch in a single sit.
Feature Detection This is a simple plementation of Harris corner detector. For each pixel $(u,v)$, we calculate a score
$$R = det(A_{u,v}) - {\lambda}trace^2(A_{u,v})$$ where
$$ A_{u,v} = \begin{bmatrix} \sum{I^2_{x}} & \sum{I_{x}I_{y}}\\ \sum{I_{x}I_{y}} & \sum{I^2_{y}} \end{bmatrix} $$ and $I_x, I_y$ are the image gradients in $x$ and $y$ direction respectively.
I_x = conv2(img, [-1 0 1; -2 0 2; -1 0 1], 'valid'); I_y = conv2(img, [-1 -2 -1; 0 0 0; 1 2 1], 'valid'); I_xx = double(I_x.^2); I_yy = double(I_y.^2); I_xy = double(I_x.*I_y); I_xx_sum = conv2(I_xx, ones(patch_size), 'valid'); I_yy_sum = conv2(I_yy, ones(patch_size), 'valid'); I_xy_sum = conv2(I_xy, ones(patch_size), 'valid'); pad_size = floor((patch_size+1)/2); scores = (I_xx_sum.*I_yy_sum - I_xy_sum.^2) - lambda*(I_xx_sum + I_yy_sum).^2; scores(scores < 0) = 0; scores = padarray(scores, [pad_size pad_size]); After calculating the score, we simply select $k$ keypoints with highest scores (with non-maximum suppression).
scores_pad = padarray(scores, [r r]); score_size = size(scores_pad); keypoints = zeros(2, k); for i = 1:k [~, idx] = max(scores_pad, [], 'all', 'linear'); [row, col] = ind2sub(score_size, idx); keypoints(:, i) = [row; col] - r; scores_pad(row-r:row+r, col-r:col+r) = 0; end KLT Feature Tracker …
Pose Estimation …
Triangulation …
The result of vo_initialize.m seems reasonable. Good to go!
Problems from Previous Implementation …
Estimate World Camera Pose …
Bundle Adjustment Bundle adjustment is a very cool concept. To put it simply, it is an optimization algorithm used to refine the estimated trajectory.
In this implementation, a motion-only bundle adjustment is implemented, which optimizes only the camera orientation $R$ and position $t$. This implies that
Results Putting it all together, the vo_initialize.m function initializes the VO pipeline, creating initial 3D point landmarks, extracting initial keypoints, and estimating the initial pose of the camera. The vo_process.m sequentially extracting and tracking image features from an image frame, across frames, and simultaneously estimating the pose of the camera. Bundle adjustment is also implemented to refine the estimated pose at each step. Lastly, new 3D points are regularly created as the number of currently tracked keypoints is shrinking over time. The following is the final result.
From the video, it is obvious that this is not a state-of-the-art implementation. There are various components that are not implemented. As we can see, the estimated trajectory starts to deviate from the ground truth after some time, due to the scale drift–a common problem in monocular VO. The estimated trajetory also wiggles slightly, probaly due to the fact that the full bundle adjustment is not implemented. And the most importantly, I did not try to implement a loop closure.
Reflections The task of implementing VO from scratch may sound lacking of excitement. I believe that the conventional pipeline of VO and SLAM is something that is already well-understood in the computer vision community. What I realize is that academic papers usually have missing steps that are left for the readers to figure out. Here, I tried to connect those steps and the result stands as a self-assesment of my understanding.
summary: Introduction This is the first-ever post of my blog; so I will give it a try. This post is about things that I went through when I tried to implement a simple monocular visual odometry from scratch.
title: Visual Odometry Implementation from Scratch

content:
This is a project where we used reinforcement learning to train the robot to collect balls in a simple environment. The robot is a 4-Mecanum wheeled robot equipped with a camera and a 2D LiDAR sensor. The algorithms were implemented on Intel NUC and Nvidia Jetson TX2 board.
This is my attempt at re-writing a write-up because a lot of recruiters ask me how the project was done and I sometimes forget (it was done in 2018).
Optimal Policy and Optimal Value Functions Bellman optimality equation
For optimal value function $v_{*}$:
$$ \begin{aligned} v_{*}(s) &= \max_{a} E \left[ R_{t+1} + \gamma v_{*}(S_{t+1}) \vert S_{t}=s, A_{t}=a \right] \\ &= \max_{a} \sum_{s',r} p(s',r \vert s,a) \left[ r + \gamma v_{*}(s') \right] \end{aligned} $$ For optimal action-value function $q_{*}$:
$$ \begin{aligned} q_{*}(s,a) &= E \left[ R_{t+1} + \gamma \max_{a'} q_{*}(S_{t+1}, a') \vert S_{t} = s, A_{t} = a \right] \\ &= \sum_{s',r} p(s',r \vert s,a) \left[ r + \gamma \max_{a'} q_{*}(s',a') \right] \end{aligned} $$ Monte Carlo Methods Monte Carlo methods only require a sample of states, actions, and rewards from interaction between the agent and the environment. It is model-free; the probability distributions such as state-transition $p(s' \vert s,a)$ need not to be known.
Q-Learning $$ Q(s,a) \leftarrow (1-\alpha)Q(s,a) + \alpha \left[ r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s',a') \right] $$ Initialize Q(s, a) Start with state "s" Loop: Select action "a" with e-greedy Execute action "a", receive immediate reward "r" and go to state "s'" Q(s, a) = Q(s, a) + alpha*[r + gamma * max{Q(s', a')} - Q(s, a)] But what if the number of $(s,a)$ pairs are very big? Then it is not practical to keep the table $Q$ for every pair of $(s,a)$. Instead, we could maintain $Q(s,a)$ as a parameterized function. This is where the neural network comes into play.
Q-Network Training
We define the loss as:
$$ L(\theta) = \left( \left( r + \gamma \max_{a'} {Q(s', a' | \theta }) \right) - Q(s,a|\theta) \right)^2 $$ Our objective is to find weight $\theta$ of the network to minimize the loss:
$$ \min_{\theta} L(\theta) = \min_{\theta} \left[ \left( r + \gamma \max_{a'} {Q(s', a' | \theta }) - Q(s,a|\theta) \right)^2 \right] $$ where $r$ is the immediate reward that we observe and the term $r + \gamma \max_{a'} {Q(s', a' | \theta })$ is the approximated target.
Convergence
However, using a neural network to represent the action-value function tends to be unstable due to:
Correlations between samples Non-stationary targets How does DeepMind solve this issue?
Experience replay Separated networks Go deeper (added by myself) Experience Replay Separated Networks $$ L(\theta) = \left( \left( r + \gamma \max_{a'} {Q(s', a' | \theta^{-} }) \right) - Q(s,a|\theta) \right)^2 $$ Gallery References Mnih, V. et al. Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning. Nature 518, 529–533 (2015).
